paragraphs: Semantic search represents queries and searchable items as vectors, then retrieves items with nearby representations. Using large vectors throughout this process can be expensive. AdANNS asks whether every stage needs the same representational capacity, particularly when some stages already tolerate approximate computation.

The framework uses Matryoshka Representations to supply different capacities for different search stages. Stages that can tolerate coarser information use smaller representations, while other stages can use more capacity. The authors apply this approach to both search structures, through AdANNS-IVF, and quantization, through AdANNS-OPQ. This makes representation size part of the search design.

On ImageNet retrieval, AdANNS-IVF reports up to 1.5% greater accuracy at equal compute, or matching accuracy with up to 90-fold lower wall-clock time. On Natural Questions, a 32-byte AdANNS-OPQ representation matches a 64-byte rigid baseline. Gains also extend to combined search-and-quantization indices. The paper further demonstrates adapting computation during inference on indices originally built non-adaptively using Matryoshka Representations.
neurips-2023-adanns-a-framework-for-adap.tldr: AdANNS varies representation capacity across search stages to improve measured retrieval accuracy–compute trade-offs.

paragraphs: Distributed count tracking asks a central server to keep track of the total number of items arriving at multiple sites while minimizing communication. Randomized algorithms have a known square-root-of-k communication advantage over deterministic approaches, where k is the number of sites. Earlier randomized methods, however, assume that the incoming streams are fixed before execution.

The paper considers a more demanding setting: an adversary can choose subsequent items after observing the algorithm's previous answers. That feedback can undermine randomized methods designed for fixed streams. The central question is whether randomness still offers its communication advantage when the input can respond to the system's behavior.

The authors provide a robust algorithm with optimal communication, establishing that the advantage survives adaptive inputs. To obtain this result, they introduce partial differential privacy and prove a corresponding generalization theorem, because existing robustness techniques do not achieve optimal bounds in this distributed setting. The theorem may also be useful beyond count tracking, although the abstract presents that broader applicability as a possibility.
neurips-2023-adversarially-robust-distri.tldr: A new partial differential privacy framework enables communication-optimal randomized count tracking against adaptive adversaries.

paragraphs: Increasing a transformer's size can improve its performance, but also raises computation costs and inference latency. Alternating Updates, or AltUp, targets the width of the representation associated with each token. Its aim is to give the model a wider representation while keeping the additional latency negligible.

At each layer, AltUp performs computation on a subblock of that wider representation. A predict-and-correct mechanism updates the blocks that are not active at that layer. This separates the amount of information the representation can hold from the amount of it receiving the layer's active computation, making widening less computationally burdensome.

The paper also explores applying the idea along the sequence dimension and combining it with Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models. Experiments across transformer models and language tasks report consistent benefits. On SuperGLUE and SQuAD, the reported speedup reaches 87% relative to dense baselines at matching accuracy. These findings support AltUp as a practical way to improve the capacity–efficiency trade-off in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-alternating-updates-for-eff.tldr: AltUp widens transformer representations through partial updates, achieving up to 87% speedup at matching accuracy on reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, the communication network influences how quickly participating nodes reach agreement. A network with rapid consensus can help learning converge, but connecting each node to many others raises communication costs. The paper addresses this tension by designing a topology that combines fast agreement with a small maximum number of connections.

The proposed Base-(k+1) Graph supports exact consensus after finitely many iterations for any number of nodes and maximum degree k. The central feature is therefore stronger than simply approaching agreement progressively: the topology reaches agreement in a finite number of rounds while respecting the degree constraint.

The authors show that this property gives decentralized stochastic gradient descent faster convergence and greater communication efficiency than the exponential graph. Experiments with several topologies also find improved accuracy and communication efficiency across various decentralized learning methods. The contribution links a concrete network property to both theoretical learning behavior and measured outcomes, showing why topology design matters alongside the choice of optimization algorithm.
neurips-2023-beyond-exponential-graph-co.tldr: The Base-(k+1) Graph combines finite-time exact consensus with limited connectivity to improve decentralized learning efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much an adaptive algorithm can overfit a test dataset when evaluated using robust accuracy in multiclass classification. The question concerns the reliability of evaluation feedback: an algorithm can use earlier answers when deciding what to query next, so its interaction with the test set is adaptive.

The analysis is organized around three quantities: the number of classes, the number of robust accuracy queries, and the number of test examples. Together, these specify the classification setting, the amount of evaluation feedback available, and the size of the dataset being queried. The target is a quantitative characterization of robust overfitting bias in terms of these quantities.

The authors establish upper and lower bounds that nearly match. An upper bound limits how large the bias can become, while a lower bound demonstrates bias that adaptive algorithms can attain. Their near agreement tightly characterizes the problem without claiming exact equality. The contribution therefore explains the possible extent of adaptive robust overfitting, rather than proposing a particular classifier.
neurips-2023-characterization-of-overfit.tldr: Near-matching bounds characterize adaptive robust overfitting in terms of class count, query count, and test-set size.

paragraphs: The paper asks which assumptions make neural networks computationally efficient to learn. Previous results established efficient learning for depth-two networks with Gaussian inputs and non-degenerate weight matrices. The authors investigate whether similarly favorable conditions are sufficient when the network becomes deeper.

For depth-three ReLU networks, they prove hardness even with Gaussian inputs and random perturbations added to the parameters. This perturbation setting, called smoothed analysis, tests whether difficulty persists after the parameters are randomly disturbed. Their result also implies hardness with non-degenerate weight matrices, showing that the earlier depth-two assumptions do not suffice for this deeper setting.

The authors additionally establish hardness for depth-two networks when both the parameters and input distribution undergo smoothing. All these hardness results depend on a stated assumption about the existence of local pseudorandom generators. Under that assumption, the findings identify limits to using Gaussian inputs, non-degeneracy, or smoothing as guarantees of efficient learning. They concern the studied learning problems rather than asserting that practical neural-network training always fails.
neurips-2023-computational-complexity-of.tldr: Conditional hardness results show that smoothing and non-degeneracy do not suffice for efficient learning in the studied neural-network settings.

paragraphs: Estimating the evolving state of a high-dimensional system can be computationally difficult, especially when its dynamics are only partly known and historical observations are scarce. This paper uses available knowledge about which state variables depend on one another. A graph captures that structure and becomes a foundation for efficient probabilistic modeling.

The authors reformulate graph-structured state-space models as Deep Gaussian Markov Random Fields. Simple spatial and temporal graph layers describe relationships across variables and across time. Together, these layers provide a flexible prior over how the system evolves. The prior can be learned from a single time sequence using variational inference.

Under linear Gaussian assumptions, the method retains a closed-form posterior distribution for state estimation. Samples from that posterior can be obtained efficiently with the conjugate gradient method. The abstract reports favorable scaling compared with classical Kalman-filter-based approaches. The contribution combines learnable spatiotemporal structure with tractable inference, while the closed-form posterior claim specifically depends on the stated linear Gaussian assumptions.
neurips-2023-deep-gaussian-markov-random.tldr: Deep graph-based Gaussian models enable efficient learning and state estimation from limited temporal data, with closed-form posteriors under linear Gaussian assumptions.

paragraphs: Diff-Instruct transfers knowledge from a pretrained diffusion model into another generative model without using training data for that transfer. Its scope includes generators whose outputs are differentiable with respect to their parameters. This condition allows the diffusion model's guidance to influence how the receiving generator is trained.

The training framework corresponds to minimizing Integral Kullback-Leibler divergence. This quantity combines KL divergences along a diffusion process instead of comparing distributions only at one point. The authors show that it is more robust when the distributions have misaligned supports, meaning their probability mass occupies different regions. They also establish connections to DreamFusion and generative adversarial training.

The experiments examine two uses: distilling diffusion models and improving existing GAN generators. Diff-Instruct produces state-of-the-art single-step diffusion-based models in the reported distillation experiments and consistently improves pretrained GAN generators across the tested settings. These results support a shared transfer framework for different generator types, with differentiability of generated samples remaining an explicit requirement.
neurips-2023-diff-instruct-a-universal-a.tldr: Diff-Instruct uses a diffusion-based distribution objective to transfer pretrained knowledge into differentiable generators without training data.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models sometimes generate pictures that miss the intended meaning of a prompt. This paper addresses that semantic misalignment by adapting the context vectors used during generation. Its approach models a posterior distribution over those vectors, giving the context update a probabilistic foundation.

The authors construct energy-based models involving latent image representations and text embeddings inside each cross-attention layer of the denoising autoencoder. They derive the gradient of the context vectors' log posterior and use it to update the context before passing it to the next layer. These successive updates implicitly minimize a nested hierarchy of energy functions.

The same formulation supports zero-shot compositional generation by linearly combining cross-attention outputs associated with different contexts. Experiments report effectiveness in generating multiple concepts, text-guided inpainting, and editing both real and synthetic images. The contribution connects prompt alignment to context adaptation within the model's layers, and uses that mechanism across several generation and editing tasks.
neurips-2023-energy-based-cross-attentio.tldr: Energy-based updates adapt text context across diffusion-model attention layers to improve semantic control and compositional generation.

paragraphs: The paper studies dataset expansion: automatically creating new labeled examples from a small dataset that is already ready for training. The motivation is that collecting and annotating large datasets is costly. Its Guided Imagination Framework, or GIF, uses generative models such as DALL-E2 and Stable Diffusion to produce additional training images.

GIF modifies latent features of the seed examples within the generative model's semantically meaningful space. Two criteria guide this process: increasing useful information while maintaining the class, and promoting diversity among samples. Together, they aim to produce new content that remains appropriate for its label and contributes useful variation to training.

The experiments find these criteria essential for effective expansion. GIF using Stable Diffusion reports 13.5% higher model accuracy than unguided Stable Diffusion expansion on natural-image datasets. The abstract also reports average accuracy increases of 36.9% across six natural-image datasets and 13.5% across three medical datasets. These findings show that guidance toward training usefulness matters alongside the ability to generate realistic images.
neurips-2023-expanding-small-scale-datas.tldr: GIF expands small labeled datasets with generated images guided to preserve class information and increase useful diversity.

paragraphs: Multilayer perceptrons offer a relatively simple approach to time-series forecasting, but the paper identifies pointwise mappings and information bottlenecks as obstacles. It investigates moving their learning operations into the frequency domain, where the representation exposes signal structure differently from a sequence of individual time points.

The authors identify two useful characteristics: a global view that makes broad dependencies easier to learn, and energy compaction that concentrates signal energy in fewer frequency components. Their FreTS architecture first converts time-domain signals into complex-valued frequency representations. Redesigned MLPs then learn from the real and imaginary components of those representations.

FreTS applies these stages both within individual series and across series, supporting learning of temporal and channel relationships. Experiments cover 13 real-world benchmarks, including seven for short-term forecasting and six for long-term forecasting, and report consistent superiority over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support changing the representation on which a simple model operates as a way to improve forecasting performance.
neurips-2023-frequency-domain-mlps-are-m.tldr: FreTS learns time-series relationships with frequency-domain MLPs, reporting improvements across 13 short- and long-term forecasting benchmarks.

paragraphs: Prototype-based explanations help describe graph neural network predictions through representative graph examples. However, a prototype that includes too much of a graph can obscure the structures that actually matter. Existing approaches may omit important substructures or retain irrelevant ones, affecting both interpretability and prediction performance.

The proposed Prototype-based Graph Information Bottleneck, or PGIB, integrates prototype learning with an information bottleneck framework. It uses this combination to identify a key subgraph from the input that matters for prediction and provide prototypes focused on that information. Prototype learning therefore participates in finding the relevant structure, rather than depending on an overly broad whole-graph representation.

Experiments, including qualitative analysis, report better prediction performance and explainability than the compared state-of-the-art methods. These findings connect the two goals: focusing prototypes on useful substructures can support accurate decisions while making their basis easier to understand. The paper's central contribution is the integration of prototype learning into the process of identifying prediction-relevant subgraphs.
neurips-2023-interpretable-prototype-bas.tldr: PGIB jointly learns prototypes and prediction-relevant subgraphs to improve graph-model accuracy and explainability in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A useful supervised embedding should respond to the label a task cares about while remaining stable under unrelated changes. This paper describes that stability through repeatability, a concept from measurement theory. It proposes the intra-class correlation coefficient, or ICC, as a way to evaluate how repeatable learned embeddings are.

The authors then turn this evaluation idea into a training component. Their ICC regularizer complements contrastive losses and encourages embeddings with higher repeatability. Simulated data illustrate why adding the regularizer reduces variation within a class more effectively than using the contrastive loss alone. The intended effect is to make representations less sensitive to confounding variation.

The method is evaluated on speaker verification, voice style conversion, and detection of dysphonic voice. In these experiments, adding ICC regularization improves embedding repeatability compared with contrastive training alone, and the resulting embeddings improve downstream task performance. The paper thus connects a measurable representation property to a concrete training adjustment and to benefits across three speech applications.
neurips-2023-learning-repeatable-speech-.tldr: An ICC-based regularizer improves speech-embedding repeatability and downstream performance in three evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Few-shot out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize images from unseen classes using only a small number of labeled examples from known classes. Prompt learning can adapt a vision-language model efficiently, but class text embeddings may retain information unrelated to those classes. That irrelevant information can make unfamiliar images harder to separate from familiar ones.

LoCoOp uses portions of CLIP's local image features as out-of-distribution features during training. Such local features can contain nuisances, including backgrounds, that are irrelevant to the known class. The method pushes these features away from the corresponding class text embeddings, encouraging those embeddings to shed irrelevant information and better distinguish known from unknown inputs.

On large-scale ImageNet out-of-distribution benchmarks, LoCoOp outperforms the compared zero-shot, fully supervised, and prompt-learning methods. It also exceeds existing zero-shot and fully supervised detection methods with just one labeled example per class. These results support using irrelevant local content already present in training images as a useful signal for learning better class boundaries.
neurips-2023-locoop-few-shot-out-of-dist.tldr: LoCoOp uses irrelevant local image features to regularize prompts and improve detection of unseen classes with few labeled examples.

paragraphs: Compressing communication makes distributed training cheaper, but the resulting errors can accumulate and destabilize optimization. Error feedback helps mitigate this problem. The paper identifies a remaining difficulty in the standard nonconvex setting: known error-feedback variants require very large batch sizes for their convergence guarantees, which can be impractical.

The proposed EF21-SGDM adds Polyak momentum to the EF21 error-feedback method. The authors show that this simple change removes the large-batch obstacle both theoretically and in practice. Under standard smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions, it improves communication and sample complexity over previous error-feedback algorithms without requiring stronger assumptions such as bounded gradient dissimilarity.

A second version uses double momentum and improves those complexity bounds further. The authors also argue that their proof technique appears novel even without compression, giving it potential relevance to nonconvex stochastic optimization more broadly. The main result gives a theoretical basis for momentum as a way to strengthen error feedback, alongside the practical improvements reported in the abstract.
neurips-2023-momentum-provably-improves-.tldr: Adding momentum to EF21 improves communication and sample complexity while removing its large-batch requirement under stated standard assumptions.

paragraphs: A time-series observation can be unusual on its own or unusual because of its temporal context. Detecting both kinds is difficult: modeling time-dependent relationships should not come at the expense of recognizing isolated abnormal points. This paper combines point-based and sequence-based reconstruction models in an unsupervised detection framework.

The point model aims to quantify point anomalies, while the sequence model addresses both point and contextual anomalies. The framework treats an observed time point as the result of two stages of deviation from a nominal point. From the reconstruction errors, it constructs a ratio-based nominality score that contributes information about how normal the observation is.

The authors combine that nominality score with an anomaly score to obtain an induced score. They prove that the induced score is superior to the original under certain conditions, so the theoretical improvement is conditional. Experiments on several public datasets report better performance than most state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the practical usefulness of combining the two reconstruction perspectives.
neurips-2023-nominality-score-conditione.tldr: Combining point and sequence reconstruction yields a nominality-informed anomaly score with conditional theoretical and reported empirical benefits.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a signal from a low-rank matrix channel whose noise profile is inhomogeneous. The recovery problem therefore includes variation in the noise rather than a uniform noise description. Although the information-theoretic performance is already understood, the authors focus on algorithms that can recover the signal efficiently.

Their first contribution is an approximate message-passing algorithm adapted to this setting. They establish a rigorous state evolution describing its behavior and show that its fixed-point equations coincide with the information-theoretically optimal Bayes equations. This connects an explicit iterative procedure to the equations governing optimal inference in the model.

The authors then derive a simple, efficient spectral method. They show that it outperforms principal component analysis and matches the information-theoretic transition. This transition result places the method's recovery threshold at the theoretical boundary identified for the problem. Together, the contributions provide both an iterative inference algorithm with rigorous characterization and a simpler spectral approach that accounts for the inhomogeneous setting.
neurips-2023-optimal-algorithms-for-the-.tldr: The paper derives message-passing and spectral algorithms for inhomogeneous matrix noise, with the spectral method matching the information-theoretic transition.

paragraphs: Policy Mirror Descent is a family of reinforcement-learning algorithms that controls how a policy is improved. In its unregularised form, it regularizes the improvement step without changing the objective function. The paper compares its convergence with policy iteration, which has a known linear rate determined by the discount factor when policies are evaluated exactly.

The authors show that the general unregularised PMD family can achieve the same dimension-free rate using an adaptive step size. Matching lower bounds establish that this rate cannot be improved for PMD or policy iteration, and that the adaptive step-size requirement is necessary to attain it. The result therefore identifies both an achievable rate and its optimality.

Their analysis avoids the performance difference lemma and also extends to inexact policy evaluation. Under a generative model, the extension establishes dimension-optimal sample complexity for unregularised PMD, improving the previous best result. The exact-evaluation theorem and the sample-based extension address different settings, connecting convergence speed with the amount of data needed for learning.
neurips-2023-optimal-convergence-rate-fo.tldr: Adaptive step sizes let exact policy mirror descent match policy iteration's optimal discount-factor convergence rate.

paragraphs: Offline model-based optimization seeks high-scoring designs using a fixed dataset of designs and observed scores. A learned proxy can guide gradient ascent toward new candidates, but predictions may become inaccurate outside the training distribution. Optimizing those predictions can consequently produce poor designs.

Parallel mentoring strengthens an ensemble by letting its proxies supervise one another. In the main three-proxy setting, each proxy supplies pairwise rankings of designs. Majority voting combines these judgments into consensus comparison labels. This uses the ranking information from all three models to support mutual mentoring.

Consensus can still be wrong, so the method adds adaptive soft labeling. Starting from the consensus labels, a bi-level procedure fine-tunes the proxies in its inner optimization and improves the labels in its outer optimization. This aims to reduce the effect of noisy supervision and produce a more robust ensemble. Experiments support the method's effectiveness. Its main contribution is a mechanism for improving collective proxy guidance despite the distribution shift encountered when searching for new designs.
neurips-2023-parallel-mentoring-for-offl.tldr: Parallel mentoring combines proxy ranking votes with adaptive soft labels to improve offline design optimization.

paragraphs: Protein engineering often requires finding mutations that improve thermodynamic stability, but beneficial mutations are scarce. Deep learning can help identify candidates, yet existing approaches become expensive as more mutations are queried. The paper addresses this computational bottleneck by changing how predictions for many mutations are decoded.

Mutate Everything uses a parallel decoding algorithm to predict the effects of all single and double mutations in one forward pass. It can also handle higher-order mutations with minimal additional computational overhead. This makes broad mutation screening more efficient by producing many predictions together instead of having inference effort scale with the number of queried mutations.

The model builds on ESM2 and AlphaFold, neither originally trained to predict thermodynamic stability, and is trained using the Mega-Scale cDNA proteolysis dataset. The authors report state-of-the-art performance for single and higher-order mutations on S669, ProTherm, and ProteinGym. These findings pair a more efficient prediction procedure with strong evaluated accuracy, supporting the use of adapted protein models for stability-focused mutation screening.
neurips-2023-predicting-a-protein-s-stab.tldr: Mutate Everything predicts all single and double mutation effects in one forward pass while reporting state-of-the-art stability prediction.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation repeatedly runs a noise-estimation network, making full-precision computation expensive. Low-bit quantization can reduce computation and memory use, but the authors observe a substantial quality loss when applying it to these networks. They identify changing activation distributions and quantization error accumulated over denoising steps as the central obstacles.

Q-DM addresses these problems through two components. Timestep-aware Quantization handles activation-distribution oscillation, while Noise-estimating Mimicking targets accumulated error. The framework considers both training and inference so that low-bit operation is supported throughout the proposed approach, rather than treated only as a change to numerical precision.

Experiments on DDPM and DDIM models report substantially better performance than prior approaches. For unconditional CIFAR-10 generation, a four-bit Q-DM achieves a FID score of 5.17 and a theoretical 7.8-fold acceleration of a 1,000-step DDPM. The acceleration is explicitly theoretical, rather than a measured wall-clock claim. The results support accounting for the changing, multistep nature of denoising when designing diffusion-model quantization.
neurips-2023-q-dm-an-efficient-low-bit-q.tldr: Q-DM addresses timestep-dependent activations and accumulated quantization error to improve low-bit diffusion generation.

paragraphs: Differential-equation-based generation involves a trade-off between sampling speed and output quality. The paper attributes differences between deterministic ODE and stochastic SDE samplers to two kinds of error behavior: ODE methods have smaller discretization errors, while stochasticity in SDE methods contracts errors accumulated during sampling.

Restart combines these properties by alternating substantial noise additions in extra forward steps with backward ODE evolution. The added noise supplies an opportunity to contract accumulated errors, while the backward portion follows an ODE. The method is designed to balance error contraction against discretization error rather than relying entirely on either sampling style.

Empirically, Restart improves on previous ODE and SDE samplers in speed and accuracy. It exceeds previous best SDE results while reporting tenfold faster sampling on CIFAR-10 and twofold faster sampling on ImageNet at 64-by-64 resolution. It also improves quality over ODE samplers at comparable sampling times. In Stable Diffusion experiments, it provides a better balance of text alignment and visual quality against diversity.
neurips-2023-restart-sampling-for-improv.tldr: Restart alternates noise injection with backward ODE sampling to improve measured generation speed–quality trade-offs.

paragraphs: Answering a video question often requires finding a small relevant portion of the video. Uniformly sampled frames can miss that evidence, while training a question-aware localizer can require costly annotations and computation. SeViLA addresses both frame selection and answering using modules derived from the same pretrained image-language model, BLIP-2.

Its Localizer and Answerer are each fine-tuned in a parameter-efficient way. In the forward chain, the Localizer selects multiple keyframes according to the language query, and the Answerer uses them to predict an answer. In the reverse chain, the Answerer produces keyframe pseudo-labels that help refine the Localizer, reducing the need for expensive moment-localization annotations.

The framework outperforms several strong baselines across five video question-answering and event-prediction benchmarks. It reports state-of-the-art fine-tuned results on NExT-QA and STAR, and zero-shot results on those datasets plus How2QA and VLEP. The contribution links selecting evidence and answering questions through mutual refinement, with experiments also examining localization and the number of selected keyframes.
neurips-2023-self-chained-image-language.tldr: SeViLA chains keyframe localization and question answering, using answer-generated pseudo-labels to refine video evidence selection.

paragraphs: The paper examines how different layers contribute to representations in sufficiently deep networks trained for supervised image classification. Its empirical finding challenges the idea that increasing depth simply keeps producing more complex useful representations. Instead, the networks separate into two parts with different roles.

Early layers build representations that are linearly separable, meaning the classes can be separated using linear decision boundaries. Later layers form what the authors call a tunnel: they compress those representations while having little effect on overall classification performance. Thus, substantial transformation can continue after useful class separation has already emerged.

The empirical studies show that the tunnel appears early in training, and that its depth depends on the relationship between network capacity and task complexity. They also show degraded out-of-distribution generalization associated with the tunnel and discuss implications for continual learning. These findings suggest that evaluating later layers only through classification performance can miss consequential changes in representation, particularly changes affecting generalization beyond the training distribution.
neurips-2023-the-tunnel-effect-building-.tldr: Deep image classifiers can develop a later-layer tunnel that compresses already separable representations and degrades out-of-distribution generalization.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether choosing neural networks or gradient-boosted decision trees is the central decision in tabular machine learning. It compares 19 algorithms across 176 datasets. For many datasets, the performance gap is negligible, or light tuning of a boosted-tree model matters more than the choice between the two model families.

The authors then examine dozens of dataset characteristics to understand when each family is better suited. They find that boosted trees handle skewed or heavy-tailed feature distributions and other dataset irregularities much better than neural networks. This shifts attention from seeking one overall winner toward understanding the properties of the data being modeled.

The findings provide practical guidance for selecting methods and allocating tuning effort, grounded in the evaluated datasets. To support further research, the authors release TabZilla, a benchmark collection containing the 36 hardest datasets from their study, together with code and raw results. The contribution combines a broad comparison with an explanation of why model choice matters more in some settings than others.
neurips-2023-when-do-neural-nets-outperf.tldr: Across 176 tabular datasets, tuning and dataset characteristics often matter more than choosing neural networks versus boosted trees.
